setup: Two credits: a BBB+ name with a 1-year default probability of 0.65% and a BBB- name with 1.25%. Were their defaults independent, the joint default probability would be only about 0.008%. In fact their default correlation is 9% (0.09).
ask: The joint default probability is closest to:

options.why: Used the independence value $\pi_1\pi_2$ and ignored the correlation term altogether.
Added $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = 0.0089$ without multiplying by $\rho$: the covariance term needs the 0.09.
Typed the correlation as 9 instead of 0.09 (percent as decimal), which makes the covariance term 100 times too big.

takeaway: Joint PD $= \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 + \pi_1\pi_2$. Even 9% correlation makes joint default about ten times the independent figure.

setup: Two credits (A- and BBB+) have 1-year default probabilities of 2.5% and 3.3%, and the probability that both default is 0.8%. Default correlation is the covariance $\pi_{12} - \pi_1\pi_2$ divided by the product of the two Bernoulli standard deviations $\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)}$.
ask: The implied default correlation is closest to:

options.why: Stopped at the covariance (0.007175) and never divided by the standard deviations.
Divided by the sum of the two standard deviations instead of their product.
Divided by the product of the variances $\pi(1-\pi)$ instead of the standard deviations; a correlation can never exceed 100%.

takeaway: Default correlation divides by the standard deviations, not the variances: with small $\pi$, $\sigma \approx \sqrt{\pi}$ is far bigger than $\pi$.

setup: A BBB credit (default probability 0.3%) and a CCC credit (0.5%) have a joint default probability of 0.02% over the horizon. You have the covariance, $0.0002 - 0.003 \times 0.005 = 0.000185$, and still need the divisor of the default-correlation formula, $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\pi_1(1-\pi_1)\pi_2(1-\pi_2)}$.

options.why: Multiplied the two variances $\pi(1-\pi)$ and forgot the final square root (this is about $\pi_1\pi_2$).
Added the two standard deviations (0.0547 + 0.0705) instead of multiplying them.

takeaway: The divisor is a product of standard deviations, a few thousandths here; the answer is a correlation near 0.05, not 0.5 or 5.

setup: Two prime counterparties each have a 1-year default probability of 5.0%, modelled as Bernoulli events with default correlation 0.5. The joint default probability is the sum of a correlation term $\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$ and an independence term $\pi_1\pi_2$.
ask: Which term dominates the joint default probability?

options.label: The correlation term, by a wide margin
The independence term $\pi_1\pi_2$
options.why: $\pi_1\pi_2 = 0.0025$ is the product of two small numbers; the correlation term is $0.5 \times 0.0475 = 0.02375$, about ten times larger.

options.label: They are about equal
options.why: Roughly equal would need $\rho$ near 0.05 (the correlation term would then be about 0.0024).

takeaway: At moderate correlation the covariance term swamps $\pi_1\pi_2$: a 5% name pair with $\rho = 0.5$ defaults jointly about 2.6% of the time, not 0.25%.

setup: Two credits each have a 1-year default probability of 2.0%. In a single-factor model with asset correlation 0.25, their joint default probability is 0.136%. Default correlation is $(\pi_{12} - \pi^2) / (\pi(1-\pi))$.
ask: Compared with the asset correlation of 0.25, the implied default correlation is:

options.label: About the same
options.why: Treated asset correlation and default correlation as one quantity. They differ: default correlation sits well below asset correlation.

options.label: Higher
options.why: Saw the joint probability (0.136%) is over three times the independent 0.04% and read that as a bigger correlation; the ratio is not the correlation.

takeaway: Default correlation is much smaller than the asset correlation that produces it: here 0.25 of asset correlation gives only about 0.05 of default correlation.

setup: A USD 1 million portfolio holds 100 equal credits, each with a 3% default probability and zero recovery. Defaults are independent, so the number of defaults is binomial with $n = 100$, $\pi = 0.03$ (mean 3). The 95th percentile of the number of defaults is 6.

options.label: USD 30,000
options.why: Used the expected number of defaults (3) instead of the 95th percentile (6); that is the expected loss, not the loss quantile.

options.label: USD 600,000
options.why: Sized each credit at USD 100,000 (divided by 10 instead of 100) before multiplying by 6 defaults.

takeaway: Credit VaR is the loss quantile minus expected loss. Here 6 defaults against a mean of 3 gives a VaR equal to the expected loss.

setup: A USD 1,000,000 portfolio has 20 positions, each with a 2% default probability and zero recovery. All 20 are obligations of the same obligor, so default correlation is 1 and the portfolio behaves like one credit: a 2% chance of losing everything, 98% of losing nothing.

options.label: USD 0
options.why: Read the 98% chance of no loss as covering the 99% level; but the worst 1% of outcomes lies inside the 2% default scenario.

options.label: USD 20,000
options.why: Quoted the expected loss ($0.02 \times$ 1,000,000), which is the mean, not a quantile.

working.label: Compare with default probability
working.display: $2\% > 1\%$, so the 1% tail sits inside the default outcome

takeaway: At correlation 1, if the default probability exceeds the tail (1 minus the confidence level), the loss quantile is the whole portfolio.

setup: A USD 100 million portfolio of credits that all behave identically (default correlation 1). Each has a 2% default probability and zero recovery. Credit VaR is the loss quantile at the confidence level minus the expected loss.
ask: At 95% confidence the credit VaR is:

options.label: Positive
options.why: Took the 95th-percentile loss as the full USD 100 million. But default has only a 2% chance, below the 5% tail, so the quantile is not the full loss.

options.label: Exactly zero
options.why: Stopped at the zero loss quantile and did not subtract the USD 2 million expected loss.

working.label: 95th percentile loss
working.display: 0, because 98% of outcomes have no loss

takeaway: Credit VaR is a quantile minus the mean, so it can be negative when the default probability is below the tail probability.

setup: A USD 1,000,000 portfolio holds 50 equal credits, each with a 2% default probability and zero recovery. With default correlation 0 the 99th percentile is 4 defaults. With correlation 1 the portfolio acts as one credit that defaults entirely with probability 2%.
ask: Moving correlation from 0 to 1 raises the 99% credit VaR by about:

options.label: ≈ USD 20,000
options.why: Quoted the expected loss; it is the same in both cases, so it cancels out of the change.

options.label: ≈ USD 60,000
options.why: Reported the correlation-0 VaR (80,000 - 20,000) rather than the change.

options.label: ≈ USD 9,200,000
options.why: Scale slip (10×): the change cannot exceed the USD 1,000,000 portfolio.

takeaway: Expected loss is unchanged by correlation; only the tail moves. Going from 0 to 1 takes VaR from about 6% to about 98% of the portfolio.

setup: A USD 600 million portfolio holds 40 equal credits, each with a 3.0% default probability and loss given default 80%. Default correlation is 0. The 99th percentile of the number of defaults is 4. You are building credit VaR as the 99th-percentile loss minus expected loss.
ask: The expected loss is closest to:

options.label: USD 18m
options.why: Left out the 80% loss given default: $600 \times 0.03 = 18$.

options.label: USD 12m
options.why: Took the loss on a single default ($15 \times 0.8$) instead of scaling by the number of expected defaults.

options.label: USD 48m
options.why: That is the 99th-percentile loss (4 defaults), not the expected loss.

takeaway: Expected loss uses PD $\times$ LGD $\times$ exposure; the quantile loss uses the defaults count $\times$ LGD $\times$ exposure. VaR is the gap.

setup: Single-factor credit model. A position has $\beta = 0.8$ and default probability 1%, so $k = N^{-1}(0.01) = -2.33$. For a loss level $x = 0.01$, also $N^{-1}(x) = -2.33$. The market value that produces that loss level is $m = [k - \sqrt{1-\beta^2}\,N^{-1}(x)]/\beta$.

options.label: Below -2.33
options.why: Added the second term instead of subtracting it: $(-2.33 - 1.398)/0.8 = -4.66$.

options.label: Positive
options.why: Flipped the sign of $k$ (used +2.33), which gives $m = +4.66$; a bad market outcome must be negative.

takeaway: Subtracting a negative term pulls the numerator toward zero, so $m$ is a milder bad draw than $k$ itself.

setup: Single-factor model: conditional default probability $p(m) = N[(k - \beta m)/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}]$. A firm has $\beta = 0.60$ and $k = -1.645$ (unconditional PD 5.0%). In a downturn the market factor is $m = -1.41$.
ask: The argument of $N(\cdot)$ is closest to:

options.why: Left out the division by $\sqrt{1-\beta^2} = 0.8$: the numerator alone is $-0.799$.
Ignored the downturn: $-1.645 / 0.8 = -2.06$ is just the unconditional threshold rescaled.

takeaway: A bad factor draw ($m < 0$) shifts the numerator toward zero; the rescaled argument near $-1$ means roughly a 16% default probability, triple the 5% baseline.

setup: Single-factor model: asset return $a = \beta m + \sqrt{1-\beta^2}\,\epsilon$, with $m$ (market) and $\epsilon$ (idiosyncratic) independent standard normals. A firm's systematic risk is 70% of its return variance and idiosyncratic risk the other 30%.

options.why: Used the idiosyncratic share (30%) instead of the systematic share.
Took the square root of the idiosyncratic share, $\sqrt{0.30} = 0.55$.
Treated the variance share as the loading itself; $\beta^2$ is the share, so $\beta$ needs a square root.

takeaway: The loading $\beta$ is the square root of the systematic variance share; $\beta^2$ is the share itself.

setup: One-factor Gaussian copula with common copula correlation 0.25, so each loading is $a = \sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$. Each company has a 10% 5-year default probability ($N^{-1}(0.10) = -1.2816$). The common factor is at its 1st percentile, $F = -2.326$. Conditional PD is $N[(N^{-1}(Q) - aF)/\sqrt{1-a^2}]$.
ask: The conditional 5-year default probability is closest to:

options.why: Added $aF$ instead of subtracting it, pushing the argument to $-2.82$ and the PD far below the unconditional 10%.
Read the factor's 1st percentile as the default probability.
Ignored the factor shock and quoted the unconditional PD.

takeaway: A 1st-percentile factor almost cancels the firm's default threshold, so the conditional PD lands just under 50% even though the unconditional PD is 10%.

setup: A Gaussian-copula simulation tracks default over 5 years. A company's cumulative default probabilities at years 1 to 5 are 1%, 3%, 6%, 10% and 15%. Its simulated standard normal draw is $x = -1.60$, and $N(-1.60) = 5.5\%$. The company defaults in the first year whose cumulative probability exceeds that figure.
ask: In which year does it default?

options.label: Year 2
options.why: Picked the last year whose cumulative probability (3%) is still below 5.5%, which is the year it survives, not the year it defaults.

options.label: No default within 5 years
options.why: Thought $x$ must fall below the 1% threshold ($-2.33$); the draw only has to fall below the year-3 threshold.

takeaway: Compare the draw with the cumulative thresholds: default happens in the first year whose cumulative probability exceeds $N(x)$.
